title: Bayer Corp. v. United States
articleTitle: The Evolution of Substantiation Standards in Federal Research Tax Credits: A Comprehensive Analysis of Bayer Corp. v. United States and Contemporary Judicial Trends
court: United States District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania
subject: Statistical Sampling for QRE Substantiation
summary: Addressed the qualification of internal-use software and the application of the discovery rule under pre-2003 regulations.

body.text: The federal tax credit for increasing research activities, codified under Section 41 of the Internal Revenue Code, represents one of the most significant and complex incentives within the United States tax system. Designed to stimulate domestic innovation and enhance global competitiveness, the credit allows eligible taxpayers to reduce their tax liability based on increased spending on research and development. However, the administrative and judicial application of this credit has historically been fraught with tension between the Internal Revenue Service and taxpayers regarding the level of documentation required to substantiate claims. The litigation in Bayer Corp. v. United States, Case No. 09-cv-00351 (W.D. Pa.), stands as a watershed moment in this ongoing conflict, involving what has been described as the largest docketed research credit case in U.S. history. With nearly $200 million in credits at stake and $6 billion in claimed research expenditures spanning nearly two decades, the case catalyzed a shift in how multinational corporations must structure their research and development data to meet the rigorous demands of the "business component" test and the "process of experimentation" requirement.
The Statutory Architecture of the Research and Development Tax Credit

To appreciate the significance of the Bayer litigation, one must first understand the four-part test established under Section 41(d). For research activities to qualify for the credit, they must satisfy a cumulative set of requirements. First, the expenditures must be eligible for treatment as specified research or experimental expenditures under Section 174. This generally requires that the costs be incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business and represent research and development in the experimental or laboratory sense. Second, the research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature, meaning it relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. Third, the research must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer. Finally, substantially all of the research activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation.

The "substantially all" requirement is a quantitative threshold, traditionally interpreted as requiring that 80% or more of the research activities, measured by cost or time, must relate to a process of experimentation. This process involves the identification of uncertainty regarding the capability, method, or design of a business component and the systematic evaluation of alternatives to eliminate that uncertainty through the use of the scientific method.
The Business Component Test as a Structural Mandate

The definition of a business component is central to the Bayer dispute. Under Section 41(d)(2)(B), a business component is defined as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention that is either held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in its trade or business. The statute mandates that the four-part test be applied separately to each business component. This requirement creates a "nexus" obligation: taxpayers must not only prove that research occurred but must specifically link every dollar of qualified research expenditure (QRE) to a discrete business component.

body.text: The administrative challenge for a company like Bayer, which operates across healthcare, material science, and crop science divisions, is the sheer volume of such components. During the litigation, Bayer estimated it had developed over 100,000 business components during the credit years in question, highlighting the friction between statutory requirements and the practicalities of modern enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems.
Procedural History and Core Disputes in Bayer Corp. v. United States

The litigation originated when Bayer filed a lawsuit seeking a refund of federal income taxes for the years 1990 through 2006. The IRS had denied a significant portion of the credits Bayer claimed, largely on the grounds of insufficient substantiation. Bayer’s internal accounting systems were designed to track costs by "cost centers"—groups of activities categorized by their nature, such as clinical studies or laboratory testing—rather than by individual research projects or business components. Bayer utilized more than 1,300 of these cost centers to organize its $6 billion in research spend.
The Denial of Statistical Sampling

A pivotal moment in the case occurred on February 6, 2012, when the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania denied Bayer’s motion to use statistical sampling to prove its entitlement to the credits. Bayer had argued that given the massive number of transactions and business components, identifying and documenting every single expense on a project-by-project basis was "unduly burdensome and time-consuming". The company proposed a plan where a representative sample of projects or cost centers would be audited in depth, with the results extrapolated to the entire claim.

The court rejected this approach, ruling that Bayer could not force the government to accept a sampling proposal without its consent. The court reasoned that statistical sampling cannot be used as a primary means to bypass the legal requirement to maintain detailed and usable records. Significantly, the court noted that the burden of identifying the business components generating the QREs remains squarely on the taxpayer, and allowing sampling would improperly relieve Bayer of its documentation obligations for the non-sampled items. This ruling underscored the principle that "practical difficulties" in recordkeeping do not excuse a taxpayer from the statutory requirements of Section 41.
The Cohan Rule and its Limitations in the R&D Context

In its effort to salvage its claim after the sampling denial, Bayer invoked the Cohan rule, derived from Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540 (2d Cir. 1930). The Cohan rule allows a court to estimate the amount of a deductible expense if the taxpayer proves that some expense was incurred but cannot prove the exact amount. However, the court in Bayer held that the Cohan rule does not automatically apply in the research credit context. A taxpayer must first demonstrate that it performed "qualified research" under Section 41(d) before a court can use the Cohan rule to estimate the "qualified research expenses" under Section 41(b). Because the "qualified research" test must be applied at the business component level, the failure to identify those components precluded the application of the Cohan rule as a primary means of substantiation. This creates a high hurdle for taxpayers: the threshold of establishing eligibility is absolute, even if the quantification of that eligibility might be subject to estimation.
The Substantial Variance Doctrine and the September 2012 Ruling

Following the sampling denial, the IRS moved for partial summary judgment, invoking the "substantial variance" rule. This doctrine prevents a taxpayer from presenting legal theories or factual bases in a refund suit that differ significantly from those set forth in the original refund claim filed with the IRS. The government argued that because Bayer was now forced to perform "Herculean efforts" to generate a list of business components for the litigation—data it had not provided during the initial audit—it was essentially presenting a new factual basis for its claim.

On September 20, 2012, the court issued a significant ruling in favor of Bayer on this issue. The court found that the "substantial variance" rule did not bar the claim because the underlying QREs and the legal theory (the research tax credit) remained unchanged. Most notably, the court criticized the government's tactics, stating that the IRS could not demand a list of business components for the first time in litigation and then object to the taxpayer’s efforts to comply with that demand. This ruling provided a critical procedural victory for large taxpayers, establishing that more detail provided during discovery does not necessarily constitute a "substantial variance" if the core of the claim was sufficiently identified during the administrative phase.

body.text: The Shrink-Back Rule: A Second Chance for Qualification

The Bayer litigation also brought the "shrink-back rule" into focus. Found in Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(b)(2), the rule provides that if the four-part test is not satisfied at the level of the entire business component, it may still be satisfied at a "subset" or a "discrete portion" of that component. This is particularly relevant in complex engineering projects where the overall product might not be "new" or "improved" in a technological sense, but specific sub-systems within it involve significant R&D.

In the Bayer case, the IRS argued that the shrink-back rule could only be used as a "second chance" after a taxpayer first failed to qualify the entire business component. Bayer countered that it should be allowed to focus its claim on the qualifying portions from the outset. While the court did not grant the government summary judgment on this point, it emphasized that the rule is intended as a safety net rather than a primary documentation strategy. The contemporary trend, however, suggests that taxpayers who fail to document research at the sub-component level may find themselves unable to utilize the shrink-back rule if their broad-level claim is rejected, as seen in the later Little Sandy Coal decision.
Comparative Jurisprudence: Bayer vs. Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner

The legal landscape has continued to evolve since the Bayer rulings, most notably with the decision in Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, which reached the Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals in 2023. While Bayer focused on the procedural burden of identifying business components, Little Sandy Coal centered on the mathematical rigor of the "substantially all" (80%) test.
The Calculation of the Substantially All Threshold

In Little Sandy Coal, a shipbuilder attempted to claim credits for the development of 11 first-in-class vessels. The Tax Court initially applied a very restrictive formula, excluding "direct supervision" and "direct support" activities from the numerator (the portion representing the process of experimentation) while including them in the denominator (total activities). This was a devastating interpretation for many taxpayers, as it meant that the time of managers and support staff actually counted against the 80% threshold.

The Seventh Circuit reversed this specific logic, providing a more taxpayer-friendly interpretation. It ruled that if an activity is research that constitutes an element of a process of experimentation, the costs for both direct support and direct supervision of that research should be included in both the numerator and the denominator. The mathematical representation of this "substantially all" fraction can be expressed as:
$$E = \frac{\text{Engaged} + \text{Supervision}_{\text{qual}} + \text{Support}_{\text{qual}}}{\text{Total Research Activities}} \geq 80\%$$
This ruling effectively lowered the bar for taxpayers to meet the 80% threshold by acknowledging that the management and logistical support of research are integral to the experimental process.
The Persistence of Proof: Shortcut Estimates vs. Principled Records

Despite the favorable ruling on the formula, Little Sandy Coal ultimately lost its case because it failed to provide a "principled way" to determine the portion of employee time spent on experimentation versus non-qualifying activities. The court held that "vague estimates" and "shortcut estimates" are insufficient. This aligns with the Bayer court's rejection of sampling: the judicial system increasingly demands contemporaneous, project-based time tracking rather than retrospective extrapolations.
Evolving Substantiation Standards: Betz and the Adaptation Exclusion

The case of Betz v. Commissioner provides further insights into the "adaptation exclusion" under Section 41(d)(4)(B). This exclusion states that any research related to the adaptation of an existing business component to a particular customer’s requirement or need is ineligible for the credit. In Betz, the Tax Court ruled in favor of the IRS, holding that the taxpayer failed to prove "technological uncertainty" at the outset of development.

body.text: The Betz decision emphasizes that the existence of technical uncertainty that requires investigative activities to resolve is critical for demonstrating that development activities are not mere adaptation. This mirrors the Bayer court's focus on the nexus between activity and component: if a project is merely "configuring" an existing product to meet a client's spec, it fails the "new or improved" mandate of Section 41(d).
Funded Research and Contractual Risks

The recent decisions in Smith et al. v. Commissioner and System Technologies, Inc. v. Commissioner highlight another critical area of R&D credit litigation: funded research. Under Section 41(d)(4)(H), research is disqualified if it is "funded" by another person or entity. The courts use a two-part test to determine if research is funded: (1) whether the taxpayer's payment is contingent on the success of the research, and (2) whether the taxpayer retains "substantial rights" in the research.

In System Technologies, the Tax Court ruled in favor of the taxpayer, finding that Indiana state law provided a remedy (such as a refund) if the research failed, meaning the payment was indeed contingent on success. This demonstrates that future applications must not only document the technical work but also the legal and contractual framework of the research projects.
Implications for Future R&D Tax Credit Applications

The cumulative effect of Bayer, Little Sandy Coal, and subsequent Tax Court decisions has created a "new normal" for R&D credit compliance. The implications for future applications are profound, particularly for large-scale pharmaceutical, manufacturing, and technology firms.
The Death of the Aggregate Cost Center Model

The most immediate implication of Bayer is that companies can no longer rely solely on aggregate "cost center" accounting for their R&D claims. While using a cost center system does not automatically disqualify a claim, the taxpayer must be prepared to create a "nexus" between those centers and identifiable business components. This requires a significant investment in data infrastructure that can "cross-walk" financial expenditures to engineering projects or clinical trial phases.
Strategic Use of the Shrink-Back Rule

The Little Sandy Coal case demonstrated that an "all-or-nothing" strategy—defining the business component as a massive, entire product—is inherently risky. Future applications should proactively apply the shrink-back rule by identifying sub-components and documenting the four-part test at those granular levels. If the overall project fails to meet the 80% experimentation threshold, the credit may still be salvaged for the specific sub-systems where research was concentrated.
Documenting the "Scientific Method"

Judicial trends indicate that the IRS and the courts are narrowing what qualifies as "uncertainty" and "experimentation". It is no longer enough to show that a product was "new" or "complex." Taxpayers must document the systematic process used to resolve uncertainty, including:

items: The initial hypothesis regarding capability, method, or design.
The specific alternatives considered and evaluated.
The iterative testing and data analysis performed.
The failure of certain alternatives as proof of a genuine "experimental" process.

body.text: The Burden of Contemporaneous Records

The rejection of "shortcut estimates" in Little Sandy Coal and the rejection of unilateral sampling in Bayer place a premium on contemporaneous records. Future claimants should implement real-time tracking of:

items: Supplies specifically used in the conduct of research, avoiding "indirect" production costs.
High-level supervision activities, ensuring they meet the "one-up" requirement and are documented as direct support of research.

body.text: Future Regulatory Outlook and Compliance Trends

The regulatory environment is shifting to align with these judicial outcomes. The Internal Revenue Service has increasingly focused on R&D credit documentation through its Large Business and International (LB&I) division's audit campaigns.
The New Form 6765 and Refund Claims

On June 21, 2024, the IRS released a new proposed draft of Form 6765, which used to be a relatively simple calculation form but is now evolving into a qualitative reporting document. The proposed changes require taxpayers to:

items: Identify the top 50 business components by QRE volume.
Provide a narrative description of the information sought to be discovered for each component.
Break out QREs by type (wages, supplies, etc.) for each component.

body.text: Furthermore, the IRS has implemented stricter requirements for refund claims, necessitating that taxpayers identify all business components and research activities at the time of the initial filing. Failure to provide this "bulletproof" narrative can result in a claim being denied by the IRS's automated "Classifier" system before it even reaches an examiner.
Section 174 Amortization and its Impact

The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act's requirement to amortize Section 174 expenses over five years (fifteen years for international R&D) has fundamentally changed the financial incentives of the research credit. Because Section 41 eligibility is dependent on Section 174 qualification, the "uncertainty" test is now the gatekeeper for both the current deduction (now amortization) and the tax credit. Taxpayers must ensure their Section 174 and Section 41 analyses are perfectly synchronized to avoid inconsistent reporting positions that could trigger audits.
Conclusion: Synthesizing the Legacy of Bayer and Future Strategies

The legacy of Bayer Corp. v. United States is a double-edged sword for the American taxpayer. On one hand, the court’s denial of statistical sampling and its emphasis on the business component nexus have significantly increased the cost and complexity of compliance. On the other hand, the victory on the substantial variance doctrine ensures that the administrative process remains a dialogue, where taxpayers can provide further detail and evidence in discovery without forfeiting their claims.

As the R&D tax credit continues to be the focus of intense judicial and administrative scrutiny, the "Bayer standard"—the requirement to link vast sums of capital to specific technological innovations—will serve as the benchmark for every major U.S. corporation. Success in this environment requires a departure from traditional "tax studies" performed once a year and a move toward an "R&D-aware" accounting culture. By integrating tax requirements into the core project management lifecycle, documenting uncertainty at the outset, and leveraging the mathematical clarity of the Seventh Circuit's "substantially all" formula, companies can navigate the post-Bayer landscape and preserve one of their most valuable strategic assets. The burden of proof has never been higher, but for the taxpayer who adopts a disciplined, project-based approach to documentation, the R&D credit remains a potent and defensible incentive for domestic innovation.
